chunks: From him, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Ali ibn Al-Nu'man and Abu Al-Mi'zzy and Al-Walid ibn Mudrik, from Isḥāq, who said:

I asked Abū 'Abdillāh (peace be upon him) about a man who sends to another man saying to him, 'Buy for me a garment,' so he seeks it in the market, and it turns out to be with him [the buyer] at the same price as what he finds in the market, so he gives it to him from his own [stock].
He said, 'Let this one not approach [it] and let him not defile his soul.'

Indeed, Allah, Exalted and Majestic, says: 'We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they refused to bear it and feared it; and man bore it. Indeed, he was unjust and ignorant.'
And if it is with him [the buyer] better than what he finds in the market, then let him not give it to him from his own [stock].
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying a good from someone you sent to buy it for you in the market?
ai.summary: Imam al-Ṣādiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between two scenarios of self-dealing: if the price matches the market rate, it is permissible but discouraged to avoid spiritual defilement (tadnīs) due to potential hidden deception; if the seller offers a better price from his own stock, he should not do so, highlighting the importance of transparency in commercial transactions. This ruling underscores the Shia emphasis on avoiding *gharar* (uncertainty) and ensuring fairness, linking commercial ethics to the broader theological concept of the 'Trust' (al-Amānah) mentioned in the cited verse.
